p: HEARTH is getting a second way out: a hatch at the aft end into Halo's next node, which cuts the depressurization run to a hundred and five seconds.
It costs three point eight million dollars and six weeks, and Amara stood on the old crate in the high bay and told the whole company so.
Afterward she handed Nadia her index card: SIX WEEKS LATE. FOUR PEOPLE OUT.
Her father finally drove up from Pueblo to see the module, and stood a while in quarter four's square with his left hand in his pocket.
Tamarack still hasn't answered about the rack that doesn't plug in.
Pavel Ruzicka. He promised Tamarack's rack would drop right in.
Odette. Safety engineer. She found the fire expert for the smoke model.
Tiago Ferreira. Test lead. He keeps the lockout tags on the test cell.
Amara Osei. Program manager. She told the company six weeks late.
Wes Harland. Chief engineer. He paced the walk to the new aft hatch.
Jun Takeda. Keeps the model. His smoke and crew runs drove the choice.
New in this chapter: Irena and Ken Mallory.

Pavel Ruzicka, Tamarack's account lead, was in the lobby at a quarter past seven on Tuesday of week twelve, before the receptionist, with a gray plastic crate at his feet. He'd driven down from Frederick in the dark. He was shorter than his emails. He had on a pressed shirt and a Tamarack jacket that had been through the wash a lot of times, and he stood up when he saw her badge.
Nadia, he said, as if they'd met. I owe you an answer. I wanted to bring it.

He set the crate on the lobby table and took the lid off. Inside, each in its own bag with a label in neat print, were a gray box with a fan grille on one end, a short cable with a different connector at each end, and two brass fittings.

Power converter, off our ground test set. A hundred and twenty in, twenty eight out. A bridge from fifteen fifty three to Ethernet, off a bench in our lab. And reducers for the coolant. He held one of the fittings up to the window. Two weekends. It plugs in now.
So that was why he hadn't written back. He'd spent his Saturdays building this.

Nadia looked at the four bags. She'd built adapters like these herself, at the avionics shop, for units that sat on a bench and never left the building. Each one here was a box FRO hadn't asked for and a connection nobody had defined. Each brass one was two more joints where coolant could leak into a cabin where four people slept.
You built all of this yourself, she said.
Who else? He was smiling. He was also watching her face to see whether it had worked.

Nadia carried the crate to the HEARTH room herself. By eight Jun had the rack open in the model, Tiago was turning the converter over in his hands, and Odette had read the label on one brass fitting and put it back in its bag.
Four more joints in the coolant loop, she said. Inside the cabin.

Tiago set the converter down. This runs warm. It's built for a bench with a fan blowing on it, and our loop is already tight in exercise. Wes looked in from the doorway, took in the room, and didn't come in. Pavel stood by the window with his jacket still on.

Nadia thanks him for the two weekends and doesn't use any of it. Instead she opens a change notice on the interface control document, the ICD, and writes it that morning with Pavel at the table: three mismatches, an impact sheet for each side. By noon they've split the work. Tamarack puts a 120 volt power card inside the rack and HEARTH's size of quick disconnect on its rear face. FRO reroutes its two coolant lines to that face, because the rack's plumbing is hard to turn around. Tamarack adds Ethernet to the rack's controller, and FRO's flight software team writes HEARTH's half. Pavel carries the crate out himself.

An agreed interface changes through configuration control: a change notice, an impact assessment on both sides, and approval from both owners before anyone builds to it. Each fix lands on the side where it costs the system least.

Tuesday afternoon Amara pulled up FRO's purchase agreement with Tamarack, signed by FRO's buyer early in the program, from Tamarack's proposal. She read the first line out loud. One air revitalization rack, Tamarack standard configuration, per proposal. Below it were a performance spec for carbon dioxide and humidity removal, delivery in week twenty two, and Tamarack's standard acceptance test. The agreement didn't name an ICD.
Jun had asked Pavel for interface data three weeks ago, and Pavel had sent it on the day he promised. By then the agreement had been signed for six weeks, and it still said standard.
He sold us his standard rack, Amara said. We bought his standard rack. Now we need a different one.

Nadia writes a new statement of work for the rework. It takes two days and three calls. It names the work on each interface, makes the ICD the controlling definition by revision, lists the data FRO gets and when, and sets six milestones, each with the evidence that closes it. Amara takes the cost from her reserve without arguing, because the gap was in FRO's paper. Pavel reads the draft and says it's the first time a customer has told him what they wanted before he built it.

In acquisition the agreement defines what's bought. A statement of work says what the supplier will do: tasks, deliverables, data, reviews, milestones and schedule, with interfaces named by ICD revision. When the agreement left them out, the fix is a modification both sides accept.
Halo's monthly program review was Thursday at one. Amara had the agenda done by Wednesday night, and the rack wasn't on it.

I'd rather bring them a problem and a fix in the same breath, she said. We'll have the fix in two weeks. She'd stood on the crate in week ten, said on schedule, and left out the word rack. Nadia had stood by the urn and left it out too. It had felt like waiting for a fix. From here it looked like something else. HEARTH's agreement with Halo asked FRO to report, at the next review, anything that could touch cost, schedule or crew safety. The rack was what scrubbed the crew's air.

Nadia asks for the rack on Thursday's agenda and takes the slide herself. Three mismatches, a change notice open, cost and date to follow in two weeks. Ken Mallory, Halo's program manager, writes it down and circles the coolant. Thanks for not making me find it, he says. Afterward Amara tells her she'd have waited, and she'd have been wrong.
In the supply process the supplier carries out the agreement, which includes reporting status and problems to the acquirer as agreed. An early report of what's known lets the acquirer plan.

Colleen had bought the second of the broker's three, the blue and white one. On Saturday it sat in an avionics shop at the Erie airport with its panel open, waiting on a new radio, and she met Nadia beside it with two coffees and one typed page.
The work order, she said. Everything this shop does to my airplane is on here. So is everything it isn't doing.

On the back of the work order Colleen had written how she'd know the radio was done. It transmits and receives on both antennas, the audio panel works on every input, the logbook entry is made, and she flies it with the shop owner in the right seat before she signs.

The radio was a week late. The shop owner had said yes to a lot of airplanes that spring. Colleen pointed at the inspector's tray by the office door, where three logbooks sat waiting for a signature that took five minutes. Every airplane in this hangar is waiting on somebody, she said. Hardly any of them are waiting on work.
When the radio arrived it didn't fit the old harness. The shop called Colleen before cutting a wire. I wanted to be mad at somebody, she said. Then I read my own work order.

Monday of week thirteen the flight software lead brought her team's plan to the HEARTH room. Four people would write HEARTH's half of the new rack link: the commands, the telemetry, and what HEARTH does when the rack goes quiet. Tamarack's firmware engineer would write the other half in Frederick. She wanted two week sprints, a working build at the end of each, and Tamarack's engineer at every demo.

Wes read the plan the way he read everything, from the bottom. The rest of this module gets a design review, he said. Then it gets built. I don't see where the review goes. The messages between the rack and HEARTH were still being settled on the change notice.

Nadia tells her yes to the sprints, inside a baseline. They draw it on the whiteboard together. The ICD and the rack's interface requirements sit under change control, and the sprints work inside them. Every backlog item points at a requirement. Each sprint ends on Tiago's bench against a rack simulator, and the design reviews get sprint results as evidence. Wes finds the review on the drawing and taps it. Fine. Show me one that works.

Agile systems engineering is a tailoring choice. In a hybrid program the iterative team works inside plan driven gates, with interfaces under control, a backlog traced to requirements, and sprint results feeding the reviews.
Wednesday Nadia and Tiago drove up to Frederick. Tamarack was a low metal building past the grain elevator, a tractor dealership once, with a clean room built into the old service bays.
Pavel met them at the door and walked them in himself.

He showed them all of it. The clean room, where two technicians were fitting the first of the rework's new parts. The test chamber. A hallway of photos, one for every rack Tamarack had flown, with the people who'd built it lined up behind it. The early photos had six people in them. The last one had forty.

Sixty one of us now, he said. Thirty eight are on your rack. I hired eleven of them in January. The old station was closing, and its racks had been most of Tamarack's work for twenty years. If yours is late, Halo buys the next one from somebody bigger. I knew that when we bid week twenty two.

At the end of the hall he stopped at the first photo. On the old station there was always an integrator. They built boxes like the ones in my crate. We never saw them. I thought that was what integration meant.

He hadn't lied to her. He'd been holding up sixty one people with a date. He'd told her it would drop right in, and he'd believed it. She'd spent five years needing a green PASS to mean what she wanted it to mean. She knew what that kind of believing cost, and who usually paid.
On the drive back Tiago had the monitoring section of the agreement open on his lap. Right now we find out how they're doing when Pavel tells us, he said. That's not monitoring. That's mail.

Nadia calls Pavel from the car, and Tiago reads him a list of milestones. Pavel agrees before Tiago finishes the list. Each milestone closes on something FRO can see: a test report, a drawing release, a build on the bench. The monthly review happens on the floor, not in the conference room. Good, he says. Then you'll see what I see.

Supplier monitoring checks progress against the agreement with objective evidence: agreed milestones and measures, joint reviews, and access to the supplier's data. It finds problems while there's still time to act.

Before they left, Pavel took them into his office. One wall was a whiteboard schedule, drawn by hand: the rework in twenty work packages, two weeks of acceptance testing after that, then delivery in week twenty two, circled twice.

Tiago counted the green magnets on the finished packages. Four. The plan said five by the end of the week. Then he read the booking sheet for the test chamber, taped by the door. Your chamber's booked the week you deliver, and the week after. Another customer.
We'll move them, Pavel said. Week twenty two. We'll make it.

Nadia asks to work the date out with Pavel, from what's already done. They do it at his whiteboard with his magnets. Four packages in two weeks is two a week. Sixteen left is eight weeks. Then the work waits two more for the chamber, and two weeks of testing and the trip down puts the rack in FRO's high bay in week twenty six. Pavel doesn't say anything. Then he picks up the eraser.

Assessment compares actual progress with the plan using objective measures, finds the variance, and forecasts from what's really happening. A forecast built with the supplier, on its own data, is one both sides can act on.

Thursday afternoon the first change notice came back with its last signature. It had gone out the Tuesday before. The flight software team had been writing against a draft all week, because the signed version wasn't there yet.
HEARTH interface change notice, routing record. Change: rack power input to 120 volts DC. Six signers, one at a time, in a fixed order. Longest wait: chief engineer's inbox, three days.

Jun had added it up. Forty minutes of work, he said. Nine days of waiting. And eleven more of these are coming. Wes, whose inbox had held it for three of those days, said every one of those signatures was there for a reason.

Nadia asks Jun to map where each notice waits. He draws the value stream on the whiteboard: six boxes, five to ten minutes in each, and the days between them in red. Every signature stays. What goes is the line of inboxes. On Tuesdays and Fridays the six signers meet for thirty minutes, Pavel on the screen, and review whatever came in. The next notice is signed in two days. Wes reads each one in the room and asks harder questions than he ever did by email.
Lean asks where value stops flowing. Here the waste is waiting, not review. Keeping every check while removing the queue between them cuts the lead time without weakening the decision.

Friday morning a note came from Helen. Halo's ground controllers had seen the new rack link on the interface list. Since the rack's software was being rewritten anyway, could they command its modes from the ground and get its telemetry once a second? It was a small thing, she thought.
Amara read it standing at Nadia's desk. Say yes. Helen took six weeks from us without a fight. Nadia had just spent a day in Frederick looking at what a quick yes turns into.

Nadia doesn't say yes yet. She and Odette assess it with Tamarack, and the assessment takes four days. It comes to two sprints for FRO, a firmware change for Tamarack, a new change notice, and a crew override, because Odette won't let the ground switch off a crew's air without one. Nadia sends Helen a priced change with a date. Helen signs it the same week and calls to say it was more than a few messages, and she's glad somebody looked.

In the supply process the supplier evaluates a request against its capability and its effect on cost, schedule and risk before it commits, then agrees a modification to the agreement. Committing first is how a supplier overcommits.

Monday of week fourteen Tiago laid the integration sequence across the conference table. The rack went in during week twenty four, right after the coolant loop was proved, because the loop couldn't be proved under load without something on it. By now Tamarack's own numbers said the rack would reach the high bay in week twenty six, whatever anybody had said out loud.

I don't need the rack on that date, Tiago said. I need something that weighs what it weighs, runs as hot as it runs, and has its connectors. I've integrated around a fake before. Nadia still had Amara's card in her badge holder, the one from the crate. Amara saw it there and didn't ask for it back. I told four hundred people six weeks, she said. I'm not getting back up there to say nine.

Nadia backs Tiago's fake. Tamarack builds the stand-in from a spare rack frame: ballast, heaters, and the new connectors, a week of work for two people. It goes in on the rack's old date. The real rack goes in the week after it lands, and nothing behind it moves. Amara signs the plan change. Tiago adds one line to it: if the rack slips past week twenty eight, the ship date moves with it, and Halo hears that day.

Control takes corrective action when assessment shows a variance. Here that's re-sequencing integration around a stand-in so the rest of the work keeps moving. The new plan goes through change control, with a trigger for the next decision.

Tuesday Pavel sent the acceptance section for the new agreement: Tamarack's standard acceptance test, run in Frederick, and a certificate of conformance with his signature. Every rack Tamarack had ever sold had shipped under that same page.
Tiago read it over Nadia's shoulder. That's how they'll know it's done. It says nothing about how we'll know, or how the thing gets here.

Nadia writes acceptance and handover from what FRO needs instead. The section grows to two pages. Every criterion traces to a rack requirement or a line of the ICD by revision. Tiago witnesses the power, coolant and data checks in Frederick, and the rack gets an interface check again on arrival before FRO signs. The handover gets its own page: Tamarack's shipping container and lifting fixture, the manuals, two spare fans, a day of training for Tiago's technicians, and the moment the rack becomes FRO's. Pavel adds a line himself: he'd like the people who built it at the unloading.

Acceptance criteria belong in the agreement before the work: objective, traced to requirements and interfaces, with witness points. Planning the handover early covers the enabling systems and support the transition needs.

Wednesday Jun had a chart of every notice so far: forty minutes of work in each, and days of waiting between the boxes. Amara forwarded it to FRO's process owner, who kept the standard procedures every FRO program started from, with a one line note: is this HEARTH's, or ours?

It wasn't only the queue. FRO's standard purchase agreement had no line for interfaces at all. Wes's cargo programs had never needed one, because Wes had always walked over to the supplier's bench and looked.

Nadia takes Jun's chart and the missing interface line to the process owner herself. The process owner spends an hour with Nadia and Jun and changes two documents. The change procedure gets the twice weekly review, and the purchase agreement template gets an interface section a buyer can't sign without naming an ICD. Both go out to every program with the reasons attached. FRO's next supplier will get the paper Tamarack didn't.
Life cycle model management defines, maintains and improves the organization's standard processes. A fix proven on one project goes to the process owner, so every project starts from it.
Thursday Halo called a schedule review just for the rack. Mallory ran it with his assembly chart on the screen. Pavel was on the line from Frederick. Amara sat next to Nadia.
The chart still had FRO's old plan on it, with the rack in week twenty two. I'd like that date back, Mallory said. Can Tamarack hold it?
There was a pause on the line from Frederick. Then Pavel, in the voice he'd sold the standard rack in: We can try for twenty two.
Amara looked at Nadia. It was FRO's date to give, and Halo was waiting for it.

She says it once, plainly. The rack reaches FRO in week twenty six, and here's why: the rate, the chamber, the test. Then what that does to HEARTH's plan, and the one thing that would move the date again, which Halo will hear about the day it happens. She doesn't say whose fault it was. The date is FRO's now. Mallory writes twenty six on his chart. On the line from Frederick, Pavel lets out a breath she can hear.

In the supply process the supplier commits to what it can deliver, on evidence, and changes agreed terms openly with the acquirer. The date FRO gives Halo is FRO's commitment, whoever sits behind it in the supply chain.

Friday of week fourteen Nadia drove up to Frederick with Jun in the passenger seat and the ICD in a folder on his knees. Revision B, six pages, the three mismatches rolled in and every notice behind them signed.

Pavel wanted it signed where the rack was being built, so they signed it on a workbench outside the clean room, Pavel first, then Nadia. Jun ran the model check on his laptop while two of the technicians read over his shoulder.

Jun's interface check on the rack against ICD revision B. Power matches: the rack takes 120 volts DC now, with the converter inside it. Coolant matches: HEARTH size quick disconnects on the rack's rear face, where HEARTH's lines are routed. Data matches, Ethernet on both sides, and so do the mounting points.
Four black lines. Jun turned the screen so Pavel could see it. Pavel put a finger on the coolant line, where his brass reducers would have gone, and left it there a second.
Halo's chart said week twenty six. So did FRO's plan, and the integration sequence taped to Tiago's wall.

Then Pavel walked them out onto the floor. His whiteboard had moved out of his office to the end of the clean room, where everybody passed it. The twenty two was gone. Week twenty six was there in his neat print, with the chamber dates under it and the stand-in's week beside them.
A woman at the frame bench looked up from a torque wrench. She was in the first photo in the hallway, Nadia realized, one of the six. Her hair had been dark then.
She looked at the board the way people look at a date they're going to spend. Then I'm riding down with it, she said. And I'm taking my week at the lake in July. She went back to her bolt.

On the drive home Jun fell asleep against the window with the folder on his knees. Somewhere past the airport Nadia counted. Thirteen weeks since she'd told her father soon. She had a rate for everything else on the board.
